title: What's the state of film industry in your country and what changes would you like to see?

commenti.body:
Canadian cinema. (Domestic film, not the Hollywood North stuff).

I’m in film and quite a lot of professionals I’ve talked to feel like funding choices are biased – it’s pretty much an East vs. West thing, where the majority of movies star Toronto even though it’s a gigantic, diverse country with so many other voices to be heard. A lot of us haven’t really seen ourselves onscreen at all — I’m talking about a collection of provinces the size of Europe lol. I’d love to see more support for the West as well as the Maritimes.

In America I wish we could have a resurgence of films like Overboard, Private Benjamin, Death Becomes Her, Outrageous Fortune, Big Business, Beaches, Practical Magic. Directors don’t know how to film them anymore. America needs more women’s films. Where’s the next The Long Kiss Goodnight or Kill Bill? Troop Beverly Hills? In this sea of cape crap and kids movies, why can’t a director and a writer come together?

Norway:

It's pretty good! Lots of ambitious films are being made (considering the small population), with Kristoffer Borgli and Joachim Trier having success internationally. The state still sponsors all film production, and most large cities have something like an arthouse cinema and pretty active film clubs.

So much is allocated to filming American movies that not enough creative cool art is made

In part also because it is maybe the most boring country on earth

Coincidentally my grandfather helped the directors guild of canada unionize and become a massive billion dollar industry in the 70s so I suppose somewhat he's to blame
[removed]

I never saw Ashes and Diamonds, which is supposed to be one of the best Polish movies. It's one of the favorite films of two of America's biggest directors Martin Scorsese and Stanley Kubrick. Then there's Kieslowski who created so many great films. The Decalogue made me cry more than any other series. The Pianist is probably the most well known Polish film, although it's shot in English and German, so maybe that doesn't count. I haven't seen Ida, which won the Oscar for best foreign film ten years ago. It's too bad Polish film goers seem to be disappointed knowing how great Polish cinema can be. 

https://www.bfi.org.uk/lists/10-great-polish-films

I'm an American. I would like for there to be more artistic and cerebral pictures, but presumably the industry will never be as good as during the New Hollywood era. Godard saw Jaws as the deathknell of great original America, and the Americanization of foreign films. Scorsese considers superhero movies a ride and not cinema. But maybe streaming will lead to more art house films being made.

I just saw 2 Norwegian thrillers by Erik Skjoldbjærg today: The original **Insomnia** with young Bad Cop Stellan Skarsgård who comes to Tromsø to solve a murder mystery, (which was pretty good) and his later **Pioneer** with Aksel Hennie (which was pretty bad)

Not an Italian but living in Italy and very interested in the film scene here. 

The biggest problem with italian cinema is that it's completely stuck in the past. You have a few modern directors producing quality films, moretti, sorrentino and guadagnino for example, but other than that alot of low effort mid-budget features are made (and a surprising amount of nepo-directors who ride off the name of previous greats - visconti, di sica etc). There's a huge market here, but most italian people interested in film have a very low bar, all they want is an Italian language film set in Italy - so many projects that go outside of the norm don't get funded.

 And the directors that make it make great films only in the theoretical sense. They study film in great detail to a point where all the films they make follow the grain, the profesors love this and will use their connections to habe these people grow further, its a cycle that needs to end.

There's a few new names floating about, which gives me hope. All in all the great historic value of italian cinema has been far to big a burden on the industry here (with all other forms of art too).

France.

Without going in the infernal labyrinth on french production system, the main problem of french cinema is still the same: its inability to produce popular movies which are also good and/or art (mainstream/popular films here are incredibly bad, and young people despise it). Good popular movie are something a lot of countries (US, Japan, South Korea...) manage or managed to do in the past, but France, not really since the 40s, and less and less with decades. To a lesser extent, France has huge difficulties to produce genre cinema (horror, SF, fantasy...) too, and when it tries, it's rarely good.

Otherwise the system has a lot of advantages (a lot of movies produces each year, no direct profitability asked, a legal status for cinema workers, a lot of subventions to festivals or restaurations...), but this system is being attacked those years, not sure it will last as such for a long time. Also, the subvention system, with all those commissions, is really harmful in terms of standardization : 90% of arthouse indie movies in France all look alike (naturalistic and grey, flat in terms of mise en scene, psychological-sociological).

Spain

There are a lot of quality films being made, new voices that are interesting and are being welcomed by critics and audience, like Carla Simon and Rodrigo Sorogoyen. But at the same time films are being homogenized, it’s kinda imposed to us the audience what is “culturally relevant” and it’s usually related to social issues. So, there are interesting films but they feel curated to fit an agenda. And don’t get me wrong, I may agree ideologically with that agenda, but the result is that even auteur films feel too safe, nothing is new and exciting. 

Besides that, there is not enough funding and support in general, and producers tend to favor series over films (which for me is damaging qualitu of the medium), but that’s been happening for a long time. Personally, I feel the audience is forgetting our outstanding films from the past, and they are losing context in result. For example Victor Erice, whom I consider not only the best spanish filmmaker but one of the best in the world, had his new film a few months ago, his first feature film in over 20 years, and the box office on its first weekend was incredibly low. 

To end on a hopeful note, people still care about films, there is a healthy low-budget film community, and even though trashing spanish cinema is a national sport here, when the Goyas (our national awards) are around the corner everyone comes together to talk about and celebrate our films, which is nice.

Loved that last Moretti film, I’m in awe at the energy and enthusiasm he still has, even when he is a grumpy old man at the same time.

I love Italian cinema, I hope new voice get their chance soon. It’s animation, but I really liked that new Zerocalcare show on Netflix

The UK.
Very healthy if you're a technician of a certain age and experience. I have lots of friends who work as sculptors, model makers, set painters, camera ops, editors etc etc all from various backgrounds and all have plenty of work (now the strikes are over).

As for actual UK films by UK production companies made by UK directors and writers with UK actors that aren't posh: not so good. 

It's increasingly a closed shop unless you went to the right schools or have family in the industry. But I guess that's the same in all the "creative" industries these days. I sincerely doubt I'd succeed in my current vocation (editor) if I was starting out now with my working class background.
Someone's got the Goldie horn...
Seems like the Super Hero era is over

I watched a preview for a patryk vega movie and it turned out the movie is by patryk vega about patryk vega. There's a genre of bad film (familiar to audiences in america) that features writer-director-star-and-financier all rolled into one person, and usually that person wears a black tank top in the movie. patryk vega was made to wear a black tank top

If you liked insomnia you might enjoy Budbringeren from about the same period. Those two films got some recognition internationally and were supposed to become something like Scandi noir, but it never really went anywhere afterwards. Budbringeren is set in Oslo and is a bit more humorous, still gritty, pretty good.

Available on the directors Vimeo
https://vimeo.com/534788850

>" France has huge difficulties to produce genre cinema. "  
>  
>I really thought A Prophet from 2009 was going to help change this.
How is French language or Quebecois cinema represented in terms of arts funding or grants in terms of Quebec’s %population or %contribution to the GDP?

> France has huge difficulties to produce genre cinema (horror, SF, fantasy…)

I don’t live in France, so I’m basing this on the limited export pipeline of new foreign releases for film nerds, but I saw two French (from France not merely French language) genre films this summer (again, release date in the U.S. I quite enjoyed:

The Power Ranger-themed horror vignettes of [*Fumer fait tousser* / *Smoking Causes Coughing* (2022)](https://letterboxd.com/film/smoking-causes-coughing/) and also

The mocku-behind-the-scenes zombie movie filmed during a zombie outbreak, [*Coupez!* / *Final Cut* (2022)](https://letterboxd.com/film/final-cut-2022/).

I don’t in any way mean to say France is producing more and better genre films. And I recognize the difference between this and the slicker production value in genre products such as those made by Disney / Marvel.

However, I live in Denver, in the U.S., and just so happened to have enjoyed a couple of French genre movies within the last few months. That alone is indicative of nothing. However I wonder how long you’ve held this opinion, because I have seen evidence of momentum in this direction.

In Singapore the mainstream film industry is basically nonexistent. For the past 10 years it only consisted of this franchise by Jack Neo called Ah Boys to Men which was about conscription. Recently he couldn't milk it any more so there's basically no more films that a majority of Singaporeans would go and watch. The only other notable director making films now is Anthony Chen who is great but people rarely watch his movies. His latest Drift is distributing in the US before Singapore.. I don't really think there's much we can do without a systemic change to the focus of the education system which pushes people to pursue science and technology rather than the arts.

Australian here. Our industry is surprisingly woeful, when you consider how many brilliant actors we have working in the US and how strong our crews are with major studios and big US productions being filmed all the time. Our actual movie output is pretty rubbish, so is our TV. I think one of our problems is writers.
Poland really punches above its own weight in film terms.

The two movie you name are able to be produced because they are comedies, which is the main popular genre in France, often with bad films. Those two films were conceived and marketed as comedies, and can only be made because those two directors have made successful comedies in the past. 

Another "genre" which could help is crime film, as there is a past history of that in France.

But a real "serious" SF/horror/fantasy/western/musical movie? It's very rare, and it rarely works – even if, as they are more exported abroad, they can seem more present in the production for a foreign eye. 

In fact this year was a special year as there were MANY attempts of that which were realeased: *Vincent doit mourir*, *Mars Express*, *Le règne animal*, *Acide*, also *Conann* in a more auteurish way...

It still little exceptions in the whole production. But in all that, *Le règne animal* gives hope, as it was expensive, rather a commercial success, and considered a good film by audience and critics. A mix which almost never happens, and could encourage other productions of the same kind.

> However I wonder how long you’ve held this opinion

It's an opinion from everyone here really. It's to the point CNC (the national subvention system) created a special subvention to genre film alone, because they were accused of never paying for any. And it doesn't work very well, the few films they helped are for most very auteurish movies "playing with the genre", rather than something the populare audience could go see in theater.

Animal Kingdom and Talk to me are my favorite australian movies and i had a similar impression to yours. There seems to be a lot of talent in australia, but it doesnt really translate into a lot of great movies.

A prophet was one of the rare link between critics and popular audience yes, that's why Audiard was so popular (as a figure) in french cinema. 

But it was still crime movie, not the exotic movie genre in France (there were a lot in 70s, still a lot today in TV), and therefore not really was young general audience is asking for.

When people ask for genre here, they really mean horror/SF/fantasy first - what people went to see in exploitation cinema back then.

We really do need to get the fuck over derivative ww2 movies that add absolutely nothing though. How much money do we spend on telling the same story over and over again that could have been spent on a more ambitious and creative project? I swear we have 3 or 4 blockbusters every single year about the exact same thing dressed in slightly different superficial clothes. 

Were these movies to actually explore the narratives, emotions and storytelling around ww2 they would be fine but none of them do. They are entertaining theme park rides telling the exact same thing ad nauseam

Agreed, det er typisk norsk å være god liksom haha. 

But I don't really think that it's a problem unique to Norway. Especially in economic downtimes, production companies have always favored safe films. I'm not sure if the production of more commercial films have any effect on the state funding all feature film projects in Norway receive.
La Chimera was excellent and really original.
thank you. I just saw your comment, and will check out the film

Luckily the Danish film scene has been great for most of my life, and pretty revered internationally. I think the Dogme 95 movement was great but I’m also happy that it’s pretty much done for. 

There’s been some great filmmakers and actors coming through these past 30 years and I think we are in a great space. 

A lot of people working internationally has really helped the quality of filmmaking, though it has lost some of that ruggedness of the 90’s/early 2000’s.

I mean, if anyone has watched the Pusher series from Winding Refn and compare that to his work today it’s a pretty staunch contrast (not a lot of neon).

I think most danish dramas has a lot to say and are often coming from a much different place than Hollywood. The most recent film I watched was the new movie starring Mads Mikkelsen and Amanda Collin, The Promised Land, by Nikolaj Arcel and it was a representation of what danish cinema can do today. 

It’s funny that Mads is Hollywood’s favorite villain but is always the leading man in Denmark.

Spain:

Summarizing.

we have several relatively established actors and directors internationally.

There is a national commercial cinema with famous people from other things that fill theaters but without much interest.

There is a good panorama of filmmakers who, although they are established and often aspire to European awards, fail to connect with the general public.

There is very good more independent cinema, I suppose it works more or less the same as everywhere else.

There is a kind of wave of rural cinema.

thanks to "Filmin" independent distributors have found a niche.

Good to see that disliking the national film industry doesn't happen only here in Argentina. Would be interesting to explore in detail why this happens over the world. Because, as for quality, is obvious that anyone from whatever country and culture can come up with something good, but then, in reality, there's clearly a quality divide between the film industries of the different countries.

As for our industry, it's been about the same for a long time. A box office hit starring Ricardo Darín every two years, bad comedies and other kinds of forgettable movies. Recently an argentinian horror movie, When Darkness Lurks, has been playing in the US, to critical acclaim. Wasn't my type of thing, but it's good to break that barrier. Hope to see more of these kinds of successes, maybe not restricted to the horror genre.

From Borgli I saw Sick of Myself in MUBI and it was truly excellent. Comedy doesn't always translate well but that one worked perfectly. The main actress was great in that, and she doesn't even have a Wikipedia page. I saw that Borgli just this year made an english-language movie, so clearly the talent was noticed.

Italy had a promising wave of new directors (Garrone, Sorrentino, Infascelli, and, to a certain extent, Zanasi, Franchi, Ponti) some 10-15 years ago, but nothing much. We do have some 'venerable masters', like Giordana, Salvatores or Tornatore, that every once in a while produce decent-to-good movies. The rest is kinda bad and I agree with you, lot of nepotism.

I am from India and they don't make any cinema here. 

I mean, they do make loads of stuff, but I don't think that type of content can be classified as cinema. 


(It's like everything is improv : the script, screenplay, what they refer to as acting, direction, cinematography ... literally everything is improv-ed on the set with a generic idea in mind. Heck, even the production is improv-ed)

Indonesia: it truly frustrates me that great films are a rarity, especially in the commercial scene. i get disappointed again and again with the emerging of so-called promising directors or locally acclaimed ones, then finding their films to be somewhat slightly better or fall into the same holes of clichés you'd find in other films. yes, we sometimes have films like The Raid, with great action and all - but the director wasn't even Indonesian! only director i might respect consistently is Edwin.
What about Rodrigo Moreno’s Los delincuentes?

Haven't seen it, was in the theaters for a very short time. Now it's in MUBI, I think. Seen good reviews overall by critics, but some others have find it very boring. In any way, it wasn't a hit at all. When Darkness Lurks did much better.
I just finished it last night and found it unique & absolutely immersive.

Chile.

Probably similar to other countries.

Government funds exist, but are escarse. Yet, most of the films are financed by them.

Because the industry is so small, salaries are low compared to, for example, Mexico. Even if almost every other job outside film is payed better.

Chilean movies tend to do well in festivals, specially if they are a so called political film or based on a famous news story.

Some arthouse cinemas, where they show national films, but there's little interest for them.

That said, it seems to me that Chilean cinema has been getting more international recognition. Mainly thanks to Pablo Larraín, Sebastián Lelio and Maite Alberdi.
I'm also from India but I feel that's not true at all.
Which obviously means that you're a lund-bhakt lol

Even I'm from India. And this is NOT true at all. 
We may have our share of problems - but what you've written is entirely wrong.
Yet another Jahil lund-bhakt lol

In the UK it’s dominated by the privately educated children of rich posh privately educated people. This results in stale movies about the lives of rich posh people or hackneyed, self-conscious trash which patronises the working class (Saltburn - hilariously - falls into both of these categories). 

The greatest British movies of all time which accurately depict British people (most of them by Ken Loach, one of them by Robert Altman - Gosford Park - and Room At The Top) understand that this is, was, and will continue to be the problem with the UK film industry.  

It’s making a shit ton of money though.

Here in Mexico we love Chilean cinema :) The Cineteca Nacional almost *always* has a Chilean movie showing, and once a year they do a cycle of South American cinema which is dominated by Chile/Argentina.
